Example 1: the square, protect S–E for D
Blue arrow: the primary path S → E → D (cost 20).
Red dashed: the failed link S–E.
Green arrows: the LFA backup S → N → D (cost 15 + 10 = 25).
Purple: the destination D. Black numbers: link metrics.
How it works: three checks for each other neighbor N
S knows the whole map, so it can check N’s own shortest path to D. All checks use a strict
1. The right side is N’s cost to D if it went through S. Strictly cheaper ⇒ N doesn’t go back through
2. N is closer to D than S. Also stops loops between two routers that both switch to backups at once
3. N’s path to D avoids router E, so the backup survives E failing, not only the link (B5).
dist(N,E) = 20 (N → D → E = 10 + 10 beats N → S → E = 15 + 10)
N is a node-protecting, downstream LFA: the best kind. S installs N as the backup next hop for D. When
S–E fails, S just sends to N; N forwards on its normal table. No tunnel, no extra label.
1. SPF gives the primary next hop E for D (A1).
2. For every other neighbor N (skip excluded ones, B6), test check 1.
3. Mark the passing ones downstream / node-protecting.
4. Pick the best one (B7) and install it as the backup next hop.

A candidate is a (link, neighbor) pair (RFC 5286
§3.6). Another link to E itself can be an LFA.
It is loop-free and downstream, but never
An LFA is a neighbor whose own shortest path to D doesn’t come back through S: dist(N,D) < dist(N,S) + dist(S,D). It is free (no tunnel, no labels) and works
everywhere, but on rings and other sparse maps there is often no such neighbor.
